title: A Moonshot For The Big Standardized Test
author: Peter Greene
summary: Peter Greene responds to a Washington Post call for an education moonshot to repair pandemic learning loss, written by researchers affiliated with testing organizations. His charge is that the proposal assumes, rather than argues, that raising annual test scores is the most important goal, quietly skipping the debate over what schools should prioritize. He objects to expressing learning in months or years, which he calls a conversion of slices of standard deviation into time, and to extra algebra periods and summer school driven by score recovery. He also points to the tension in reform rhetoric about whether parents know their children best or are deluded, and compares the pitch to a used-car salesman who assumes the sale. His conclusion is that the testing industry needs the moonshot to rescue itself, while schools and parents should first ask what students actually need.
points: The piece treats test scores as the unquestioned objective, which Greene calls the sales technique of assuming the sale.
Learning measured in months or years is a statistical conversion, not a real unit of learning, and should set off a bullshit detector.
The authors' affiliations with test manufacturers shape the remedy, which conveniently makes assessments the center of recovery.
Score-driven fixes such as extra algebra or lost summers crowd out things like band and chorus that also suffered during the pandemic.
The pandemic showed teachers and parents did not need annual tests to know how students were doing.
quotes: Yeah, the reason that sort of investment would be historic is the same reason that unicorns pooping rainbows in the middle of Wall Street would be historic.

There is no such thing as learning measured in years, months, days or minutes. The time units of learning is a made-up sexy way to talk about--again--drops in test scores. It's a conversion made up to turn slices of standard deviation into units of time. It's a way to distract from the suggestion that of all the things you could worry about when it comes to the education, the thing you should worry most about is their score on the Big Standardized Test.
Any time someone starts talking about days, weeks, months of learning, your bullshit detector should start clanging like a Don't Fear The Reaper cowbell.

Which are exactly the kind of solutions you come up with if you start with the premise that nothing is more important than raising those test scores. And not, say, deciding that your band and chorus need extra periods to help build the ensemble skills that have suffered from the long break.

Look. This piece touts the value of transparency, but it also uses a trick known as the used car lot world as "assume the sale." That's when the salesman starts talking as if your decision to buy the car is already a done deal, and you're just haggling over details.

Testocrats are nervous. During the pandemic, testing was suspended, and parents and teachers did not collapse, wailing, "How shall I ever know how these children are doing??" Not a teacher in the country said, "Man, I wish test prep and administration was sucking up more of my time.

Either way, they need a moonshot not to rescue children, but to rescue their own industry. In the meantime, schools and parents should be having a conversation about what students need without jumping to the assumption that nothing could be more important than getting those test scores back up.
